answer.label: Spoken by

answer.sourceLine: Confirmed genuine. Sally Ride said this word-for-word in her 20 November 1998 interview on Scholastic’s website ↗, answering a student’s question about what the stars look like from space. It opens a longer answer comparing the shuttle’s view to standing on “a very, very high mountain.”

source.heading: The source

docMeta.dd: Answering “What do the stars look like from space? Are they bigger?”

source.excerpt: The stars don’t look bigger, but they do look brighter. When you’re on Earth, if you go to the top of a mountain, the stars look much brighter than they do at sea level. And because the space shuttle is above Earth’s atmosphere, it’s like being on a very, very high mountain. So they look brighter, but not bigger.
trail: The phrase appears verbatim as the first sentence of Sally Ride’s answer in her Scholastic interview ↗.
Wikiquote ↗ lists the fuller passage and cites the same “Interview at Scholastic’s Web site (20 November 1998).”
The Dictionary of Science Quotations ↗ also traces the line to that 1998 Scholastic interview.
source.excerptNote: The popular one-line quote is the opening sentence of this fuller answer — genuine, just usually trimmed of the mountain explanation that follows.

author.bio: Sally Kristen Ride (1951–2012) was an American physicist and NASA astronaut who, aboard Challenger on mission STS-7 in June 1983, became the first American woman in space. After leaving NASA she became a professor of physics at UC San Diego and co-founded Sally Ride Science to encourage young people — especially girls — in STEM.

misattribution.heading: Is it really hers?
misattribution.intro: Sally Ride’s name is a magnet for feel-good, unsourced quotes — so this one deserves a check. It passes. The wording is genuine; the only distortion is that quote sites strip away the explanation that made it a real answer rather than a slogan.

items.why: The exact sentence appears as the opening of her answer in the 1998 Scholastic interview ↗ — not a paraphrase.
Sites like Goodreads ↗ and BrainyQuote present the line alone, dropping her point that the shuttle is like standing on “a very, very high mountain” above the atmosphere.

misattribution.truthLine: A rare genuine one: Sally Ride really said it, verbatim, in her 20 November 1998 Scholastic interview ↗.

context.heading: Why it stuck
lead: Ride was answering a student, not composing an aphorism — which is part of why the line lands. She takes a common intuition (space must make everything look huge and dramatic) and gently corrects it with physics: the stars aren’t nearer, so they aren’t bigger; there’s just less air in the way, so they’re brighter.
context.pull: So they look brighter, but not bigger.
